Every entry in the lexicon already includes a base-R version of its simulation under **Show simulation code**. These four **Try it in R** pages go a step further: they are hands-on labs that run R directly in your browser with [webR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) (R compiled to WebAssembly), with nothing to install.

Each lab breaks a core idea from the [Start here](../start-here.qmd) tour into small, editable steps, gives you concrete **Predict → Modify → Observe** experiments to try on the code, and ends with a short **Your turn** coding exercise with a hint and a worked solution.

::: {.callout-tip title="The four-step fake-data workflow in R"}
Throughout his books and blog posts, Andrew Gelman advocates **fake-data simulation** as the best way to understand what a statistical method actually does before trusting it on real data. Every lab here follows the same four-step pattern in base R:

1. **Fix the known truth.** Choose numbers for the true parameters (`theta <- 0.2`, `sigma <- 0.5`, `tau <- 0.1`) so you know the right answer in advance.
2. **Simulate one fake dataset.** Draw random data from that world (`rnorm()`, `rbinom()`) and plot it to see what a single study looks like.
3. **Apply the estimator or filter.** Run the rule under study (`abs(est) > 1.96 * se`, regression, partial pooling) and compare its answer with the known truth.
4. **Repeat across many worlds.** Wrap the single study in `replicate()` or `sapply()` to measure long-run exaggeration (Type M error), wrong-sign claims (Type S error), or out-of-sample fit.
:::

## Labs in recommended order

Start with Lab 1 and use the links at the bottom of each page (or the sidebar) to step through the sequence. The first lab you open downloads R into your browser (~30 MB), which takes up to a minute once and is cached after that.
